title: What are the challenges of microservices vs a monolithic application?
shortTitle: Challenges of microservices versus a monolithic application
keyPoints: A monolith is one deployable unit with in-process calls and local ACID transactions, simple but scales only as one block.
Microservices split that unit into independently deployable services, each owning its own database and communicating over the network.
Distributed transactions are replaced by the Saga pattern with compensating actions and eventual consistency.
Partial failure and latency require timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and bulkheads on every remote call.
Observability needs distributed tracing with a shared traceId because a single stack trace no longer tells the whole story.
Operational complexity multiplies: many pipelines, service discovery, config servers, versioned contracts, and container orchestration.
Microservices are justified only when teams need independent deployment and scaling; otherwise you get a distributed monolith.

s1_definition.oneliner: Monolith is simple but scales as one block; microservices scale and deploy independently but pay with network failure, eventual consistency, and operational complexity.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Monolith** – a single deployable unit where all modules share one process, one codebase, and one database, so calls are in-process and transactions are local ACID.
- **Microservices** – independently deployable services, each owning its own database and communicating over the network.
- **Core trade-off** – the split trades the simplicity of local calls and local transactions for independent scaling and deployment.
- **Distributed-system cost** – network latency, partial failure, eventual consistency, data duplication, distributed tracing, and operational complexity.
- **Decision criterion** – microservices are justified only when teams genuinely need independent deployment and scaling.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India as one giant building where every clerk sits in the same hall. If Rajesh wants a transfer, one clerk walks three steps to the ledger desk and the cashier desk: fast, simple, and if the building is open everything works. That is a monolith. Now imagine the bank splits into separate buildings across the city: an Account building, a Payment building, a Notification building. Rajesh's transfer now needs a courier to carry forms between buildings. Couriers get stuck in traffic (network latency), sometimes a building is closed (partial failure), and you cannot lock all ledgers at once (no single transaction). You gained the ability to rebuild the Payment building without shutting the Account building, but you now have to manage a whole city.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A monolith is a single deployable unit where all modules share one process and one database, so a transfer from Rajesh to Priya at National Bank of India is just one local transaction and one stack trace tells you everything. It is simple to build, test, and debug, and it is the right choice for a small team or an early-stage product. The problem is that it scales only as one block, every change redeploys the whole thing, and one memory leak can take down the entire application.

Microservices split that unit into independently deployable services, each owning its own database and talking over the network. The biggest challenge is that there is no distributed transaction across services, so you use the Saga pattern with compensating actions and accept eventual consistency. The second challenge is partial failure: a local method call never half-works, but a network call can time out or hang, so you wrap every remote call with a timeout, a retry, and a circuit breaker. The third challenge is observability: one request now crosses three or four services, so you propagate a single traceId and view the waterfall in Zipkin. The fourth is operational complexity: many services mean many pipelines, service discovery, config servers, and container orchestration.

The honest senior-level point is that microservices are only worth this cost when teams genuinely need independent deployment and scaling. If they do not, you end up with a distributed monolith that has all the operational pain and none of the benefit.

Remember one sentence: microservices trade the simplicity of in-process calls and local transactions for independent scaling and deployment, and you pay with distributed transactions, partial failure, observability, and operational complexity.
